kurz: Why the US has no tax-free holding period, how crypto, physical gold, gold ETFs and collectibles are taxed, and which transactions count as a sale.

bloecke.md:
So far, this module has mostly dealt with stocks, bonds and funds. Bitcoin, a gold bar, a painting or a balance in a foreign currency follow largely the same US rules, with a few important differences. There is no holding period after which a gain becomes tax-free. The holding period only decides the rate: gains on assets held for more than one year are long-term and get the 0%, 15% or 20% rates, while gains on assets held for one year or less are taxed as ordinary income at up to 37%.

A second line runs through the tax code. **Collectibles**, which include gold, silver, coins and art, are taxed on long-term gains at up to 28% instead of 20%. In addition, for many of these assets nobody sent a Form 1099 until recently. Reporting them is your responsibility.

bloecke.unter: The classification of the asset determines the rate on long-term gains; the outward form of the product, such as a share traded on an exchange, plays no role.

bloecke.md:
## Holding period and lot identification

An asset is held long-term if it was held for **more than one year**. The count starts on the day after the purchase and includes the day of the sale, so an asset bought on March 10, 2025 is long-term if it is sold on March 11, 2026 or later. What counts are the trade dates, not settlement. Each purchase is a separate lot with its own holding period and its own basis.

When only part of a holding is sold, the lots sold have to be identified. Without a specific identification at the time of sale, the units bought first count as sold first. For digital assets, the IRS has required since January 1, 2025 that this be done separately for each wallet or account, not across all holdings combined. Unlike a brokerage account for stocks, a self-custody wallet keeps no books, so the allocation has to come from your own records.

bloecke.titel: No exemption threshold, but a 0% bracket
bloecke.md: US law has no small-amount exemption for investment gains. Every taxable sale, even a $5 coffee paid for with bitcoin, has to be reported. The relief lies elsewhere: long-term gains and qualified dividends that fit within the 0% bracket are tax-free. For a single filer in 2026, this bracket runs up to a taxable income of $49,450. Unlike a threshold, it works as a slice. The part of the gain above it is taxed at 15%, the part below stays at 0%. In years with low income, for example in early retirement before Social Security starts, realizing gains up to the limit can make arithmetical sense.

bloecke.titel: Tax on a long-term gain with $40,000 of other taxable income
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for a single filer in 2026, excluding state tax. The first $9,450 of gain still fits within the 0% bracket; only the part above it is taxed at 15%.

bloecke.md:
## Taxation of crypto assets

Since IRS Notice 2014-21, virtual currencies have been treated as property for US tax purposes, not as currency. Today the tax code calls them **digital assets**. Every transaction in which you give up a digital asset in exchange for something else counts as a sale or exchange, for example in these cases:

- When [[Bitcoin|bitcoin]] is exchanged for ether, the bitcoin is sold at its value on the day of the exchange, and the ether is acquired with a new basis and a new holding period.
- Paying for goods or services with a digital asset is a sale at its value at the time of payment, even for small amounts.
- A detour via a [[Stablecoin|stablecoin]] changes nothing, because the stablecoin is itself a digital asset.

Buying with dollars, holding, and moving coins between your own wallets are not taxable. A gift is not a sale for the giver; the recipient generally takes over the giver's basis, and gifts above the annual exclusion fall under the federal gift tax rules.

Ongoing income is ordinary income. Staking rewards are taxable when you gain control over them, at their fair market value at that time (Rev. Rul. 2023-14). Mining rewards and airdrops are treated in the same way. That value becomes the basis of the coins received, and their holding period starts then. When they are sold later, only the change in value since receipt is a capital gain or loss.

Even though no tax is withheld, the IRS learns about the transactions. Every Form 1040 asks at the top whether you received, sold, exchanged or otherwise disposed of a digital asset during the year, and answering no after such transactions is a false statement. Brokers that hold digital assets for customers report gross proceeds of sales on the new Form 1099-DA for transactions from 2025, and cost basis for assets acquired from 2026 onward. A rule that would have extended this reporting to decentralized platforms was repealed by Congress in 2025. For earlier years, the IRS has used court-approved John Doe summonses to obtain customer records from exchanges.

Investors who did not report past transactions can file amended returns. The IRS can generally assess additional tax for three years after filing, for six years if more than 25% of gross income was omitted, and without time limit in the case of fraud.

## Physical and exchange-traded gold

Physical gold and silver, bullion coins and most other precious metals are **collectibles** under 26 U.S.C. § 408(m). A sale within one year is taxed at ordinary rates. After one year, the gain is long-term, but it is taxed at your ordinary rate with a maximum of 28%, not at 15% or 20% (§ 1(h)(4)). For someone in the 24% bracket, the collectible rate is therefore 24%; only from the 32% bracket upward does the 28% cap matter. Some states charge sales tax on purchases of bullion, while many exempt it.

The form of a product does not change this. Exchange-traded products that hold physical metal in a grantor trust are treated as if you owned the metal directly. Their shares are collectibles, and a long-term gain is taxed at up to 28%, not 20%. The trust also sells small amounts of metal during the year to pay its expenses, which produces small taxable gains or losses for you. Funds that hold gold mining stocks, by contrast, are ordinary capital assets. Funds that hold gold futures follow different rules again: futures contracts are marked to market at year-end, and their gains count as 60% long-term and 40% short-term regardless of the holding period (26 U.S.C. § 1256). Such funds often report on Schedule K-1.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for a single filer with taxable income below $545,500, excluding the 3.8% NIIT and state tax. In the 24% bracket, the collectible rate equals the ordinary rate; in the 35% bracket, the 28% cap applies.

bloecke.md:
## Collectibles, personal-use property and foreign currency

The rules for gold also apply to art, antiques, stamps, most coins, gems, rugs and alcoholic beverages such as wine: long-term gains are taxed at up to 28%. A non-fungible token can also fall under this rule if it represents a collectible; the IRS looks through to the underlying asset (Notice 2023-27).

Two special features must be noted. First, a gain on property held for personal use, such as a classic car or a watch you wear, is taxable, but a loss on it is not deductible. The loss on selling a used family car therefore has no tax effect, while the gain on a classic car is taxed. Losses on collectibles are only deductible if you held them as an investment. Second, a balance in a foreign currency is not money for US tax purposes, but property. Gains and losses from exchange rate changes on foreign currency held for investment are generally ordinary income or loss under 26 U.S.C. § 988, realized when the currency is converted or spent. For personal transactions, such as currency left over from a trip, exchange gains of up to $200 per transaction are excluded (§ 988(e)).

Crypto and gold losses are not kept in a separate pot. All capital gains and losses of a year are netted: short-term against short-term, long-term against long-term, then the two results against each other. Losses left over after netting within a group reduce the most highly taxed gains first, which are those in the 28% collectibles group. A crypto loss of $10,000 can therefore offset a stock gain of the same amount. A net loss reduces ordinary income by up to $3,000 a year, and the rest is carried forward without time limit.

The wash sale rule of 26 U.S.C. § 1091 refers to stock and securities. Under current law, it does not apply to crypto held directly, so a sale at a loss followed by an immediate repurchase is recognized. Proposals to change this have been made repeatedly, so the rule should be checked before relying on it.

The rules above apply to investors. Someone who buys and sells so frequently, regularly and continuously that it amounts to a business may qualify as a trader, and someone who sells to customers from an inventory is a dealer. A trader in securities can deduct business expenses and, with a timely election under 26 U.S.C. § 475(f), treat gains and losses as ordinary, without the $3,000 limit and without the wash sale rule. A dealer in coins or bullion has ordinary business income that is also subject to self-employment tax. There are no fixed numerical limits. Courts look at the number and frequency of trades, the holding periods and whether the activity is the taxpayer's main source of income. Holding and occasionally selling your own crypto or gold as a rule remains investing.

For these assets, there is often no complete tax form. Form 1099-DA only covers what a broker holds for you, and for assets acquired before 2026 it usually shows no basis. Sales go on Form 8949 like other capital assets. Only what is documented will stand up. This includes the complete transaction history for each exchange and wallet, the value in dollars at the time of each transaction and the fees, which add to basis or reduce proceeds. If you cannot prove your basis, the IRS can treat it as zero, and the burden of proof lies with you.

mitnehmen: The US has no tax-free holding period; a holding period of more than one year only decides between ordinary rates and the lower long-term rates.
Gold, silver, coins, art and physically backed metal ETFs are collectibles, whose long-term gains are taxed at up to 28% instead of 20%.
Exchanges between crypto assets, paying with crypto and swaps into stablecoins are sales, even if no dollar appears in the account.
Staking, mining and airdrops are ordinary income when received; their value at that time becomes the basis for a later sale.
Crypto and gold losses are netted with all other capital gains and losses, and under current law the wash sale rule does not apply to crypto held directly.

begriffe.text: Term used in the tax code for crypto assets, stablecoins and non-fungible tokens recorded on a distributed ledger. For tax purposes they are property, so every sale, exchange or payment with them is a taxable disposition.

Asset listed in 26 U.S.C. § 408(m), such as art, antiques, gems, stamps, most coins, alcoholic beverages and precious metals. Long-term gains on collectibles are taxed at the ordinary rate, but at most 28%.

Gain on a capital asset held for more than one year, counted from the day after the purchase. It is taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%, or at up to 28% for collectibles; gains on assets held one year or less are taxed at ordinary rates.
Information return on which brokers report sales of digital assets, with gross proceeds for transactions from 2025 and cost basis for assets acquired from 2026 onward.
Regulated futures contract or certain option that is marked to market at year-end. Gains and losses count as 60% long-term and 40% short-term regardless of the holding period.
